voice.text: Before China, there was Chicago.
Dawn was a daughter and a sister. A former flight attendant. An artist who loved fashion, and travel.
Her brother describes her as intelligent, and trusting. She and their mother liked to enter sweepstakes, he told Reuters.
She came from a family of Chicago police officers. Her father, Gene, served thirty-two years. Tim served twenty-eight. Their mother and three uncles had been officers too, the commission was told.
Then an email told her she'd won.

voice.say: She received an email stating that she had won an all-expenses-paid trip to Hong Kong. She didn't believe it at first, but checked on the company and believed they were legitimate.
voice.who: Tim Hunt, CECC hearing of 18 Sep 2024 (V01 not in hand: GPO transcript S5, shown as words, never voiced), l.648-651

voice.text: On paper, the prize is cash. Out loud, it's a trip. Two descriptions of one email, both from her brother.

voice.text: She sent them her passport details, Tim wrote. They sent her a ticket.

voice.text: The words matter. It was a suspended death sentence, not an order for her immediate execution. It was later reduced to life in prison.

China sees a serious crime. In 2026, its foreign ministry told Reuters that she and another American are serving sentences for serious drug-related crimes, handled according to the rule of law, with their health and legitimate rights protected.
Her family insists she was what investigators call a blind mule: someone who carries drugs for traffickers without knowing it.
According to her family, and to reporting on the court's reasoning, the judge recognised that she had been deceived, and concluded that she should have known anyway.
Deceived.

voice.text: And guilty anyway.

voice.text: In June 2024, her brother was let in to see her.
Guangdong Women's Prison. It had taken him six to eight months to get permission.
He found a sister who had lost weight, and was very pale.

Doctors who examined her in prison, he said, had found uterine fibroids, and possibly ovarian cancer: not a confirmed diagnosis. She had needed numerous transfusions for heavy bleeding, and had been advised to have a hysterectomy. She refused, out of distrust.
She still had to work, he said, making lithium batteries.

voice.text: Gene Hunt was, in his son's words, an American of Americans. He had served in the Army, worked as a skimmer in the steel mills, and driven a Chicago bus, before thirty-two years in the police.
As a boy, Tim wrote, he watched his father save the next-door neighbours from a house fire.
There was one person Gene could not bring home.

voice.say: I will get my daughter back as I'm talking to you. She will return to me.
voice.who: Gene Hunt, NBC 5 Chicago, 19 Sep 2024 (IN-14 135.76-144.54)

voice.text: In May 2025, Tim says, the United States asked for her release on humanitarian grounds. That September, a bipartisan bill was introduced in Congress, named for her and for Nelson Wells Junior, another American held in China.
None of it brought her home.
On January 25th, 2026, four hundred and ninety-four days after that first hearing, Gene Hunt died. He was ninety-two.

voice.text: In September, he sat before the commission again.
Some things had improved, he told them. More visits. A few books.
He described a sister who had aged dramatically: slumped over, frail, her teeth yellowed and shifted, her hair much greyer.
Two years earlier, he had spared his father some of the details. Now there was no father to spare.
But there was one thing she kept coming back to.

Now she's the one asking. And no one has given her a date.
Her yes. Her letter. Her question. Every word of Dawn's in this film has reached you the same way: through her family.
As of November 2026, Dawn Michelle Hunt is still in prison in China. Her family is still asking for her release on humanitarian grounds.
